Greek literature and thought form one of the foundations of Western culture, and their influence reached the Islamic world, whose scholars translated Aristotle, Galen and Euclid into Arabic in the 8th to 10th centuries. The New Testament and the theology of the early Church were written in Greek, which remains the language of the liturgy of the Greek Orthodox Church.

For centuries, the study of ancient Greek was at the heart of education in Europe, and it is still taught in schools and universities around the world, keeping open a direct line to the words of Homer, Sophocles, Plato and Aristotle.

Hawaiian society rested on a hierarchy of chiefs (aliʻi), priests and commoners (makaʻāinana), bound by the religious restrictions of the kapu system and organised in land divisions, ahupuaʻa, that ran from the uplands to the sea, where irrigated taro, fishponds and fishing fed a dense population. Contact with the wider world transformed this economy. Kamehameha I kept the export of sandalwood to China as a royal monopoly; after his death the chiefs bought ships and goods on credit, a tax payable in sandalwood was imposed in 1826 to meet their debts, and by the 1830s the trade had collapsed. From 1819 American whaling ships called for provisions, and in the peak years of the 1840s and 1850s hundreds a year put in at Honolulu and Lahaina. Sugar grew from the plantation founded at Kōloa on Kauaʻi in 1835 into the dominant industry, worked by contract labourers from China from 1852, from Portugal’s Atlantic islands from 1878 and, in large numbers, from Japan from 1885. Introduced diseases devastated the Hawaiian people: a census of 1832 counted about 130,000 inhabitants, a smallpox epidemic in 1853 killed thousands, and in 1890 only some 40,600 of the kingdom’s 89,990 people were Native Hawaiian. Mission schools nonetheless spread literacy in Hawaiian with remarkable speed.

The power of the Tuʻi Tonga rested on command of the sea. Large double-hulled canoes carried chiefs, warriors and tribute between Tongatapu, Haʻapai, Vavaʻu and the islands beyond, and Tongan expeditions carried war to neighbouring archipelagos. On ʻUvea (Wallis), Tongan chiefs built fortified settlements such as Talietumu, enclosed by stone walls and usually dated to around the fifteenth century. Samoan tradition recalls a period of Tongan domination that ended when Savea and his kinsmen drove out the Tongan ruler Talakaifaiki, traditionally in the thirteenth century, and holds that the Malietoa title, one of Samoa’s paramount titles, arose from words of praise spoken by the departing Tongans. Violence also struck at the heart of the dynasty: tradition records that the Tuʻi Tonga Havea I, Havea II and Takalaua were assassinated, and that Takalaua’s son Kauʻulufonua I pursued his father’s killers from island to island before reorganising royal power. In later centuries warfare increasingly pitted Tongan chiefs against one another. After the assassination of the Tuʻi Kanokupolu Tukuʻaho in 1799 the islands fell into civil wars fought from fortified villages, and in 1806 the Haʻapai chief Fīnau ʻUlukālala seized the British ship Port-au-Prince at Lifuka, sparing the young William Mariner, whose later account is a major source for the period, and turned its guns to his own campaigns.

Nan Madol is the Saudeleur’s enduring monument and one of the most remarkable archaeological sites in the Pacific. Nearly a hundred artificial islets of stacked basalt columns and coral fill, separated by tidal canals, cover an area of about 1.5 by 0.5 kilometres on the reef. Uranium-thorium dating of coral from the tomb of the first ruler of the whole island places the start of monument building there at about 1180–1200, before the monumental construction that began on other Pacific islands between about 1300 and 1600, and most of its palaces, temples and tombs were built between about 1200 and 1500. The Saudeleur era also left a political legacy. Pohnpeians remember it as the first time the island was united under one government, and the customs of tribute and feasting at funerals and other celebrations are traced to Saudeleur practice. The Nahnmwarki system that replaced it, with chiefdoms each headed by two principal chiefs, still structures customary life on the island. German and Japanese colonial officials dug at Nan Madol in the early twentieth century. The site became a United States National Historic Landmark in 1985, and in 2016 it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger, because silting canals and spreading mangroves threaten its walls.

Rapa Nui was a chiefdom rather than a state with formal institutions. Highest in rank stood the ariki mau, the paramount chief, drawn from the Miru clan, which was traditionally associated with the kingship and claimed descent from Hotu Matuʻa. His authority was above all sacred: he embodied the mana of the founding line and presided over ritual, while the chiefs of each mata organised land, labour and feasting within their territories. Missionaries in the 1860s recorded that the ariki had held great power over nine other clans and their chiefs. Priests and specialists kept genealogies, chants and the knowledge of rongorongo. In the later period another institution gained importance: the birdman rite at Orongo, on the south-western tip of the island, dedicated to the god Makemake. Each year men of rank chose men of lower status, hopu, to swim to the islet of Motu Nui and wait for the first egg of the sooty tern; the sponsor whose hopu brought it back became tangata manu, the birdman, for a year, received tribute and lived in seclusion, while his clan gained rights over the season’s eggs and fledglings on the islet. The rite lasted into the 1860s, and the names of 86 birdmen were later recorded. After the old order collapsed, missionaries had Atamu Tekena of the Miru appointed king in 1883.

Chavín was the first Andean religious tradition to spread across much of Peru. Its art, with intricate fanged beings, interlocking motifs and what John Rowe called ‘kennings’, visual metaphors in which hair becomes snakes and other body parts are drawn as fanged mouths, appears in local versions at Kuntur Wasi and Pacopampa in the northern highlands, on remodelled temples of the coast and on painted cotton textiles from Karwa near Paracas on the south coast. Archaeologists use this spread to define the Early Horizon, the first of the great horizons of Andean prehistory. Julio C. Tello, who worked at the site from 1919, saw Chavín as the ‘mother culture’ of Andean civilisation. That view is no longer held in its original form, since older temples are now known on the coast and in the highlands, but Chavín remains central to the story of how shared religion linked distant Andean peoples. Its staff-bearing god, carved on the Raimondi Stela, is often compared with the staff gods of later traditions such as Tiwanaku and Wari. Chavín de Huántar became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985, and the Tello Obelisk and other sculptures are kept in the nearby Museo Nacional Chavín.

Chimor was the largest Andean state before the Incas and the last great kingdom of the coast. Its craftsmen produced some of the finest metalwork of the ancient Americas, including gold and silver beakers, ear ornaments and ceremonial regalia, as well as featherwork, tapestry and the black moulded pottery that spread with Chimú rule. These skills outlived the kingdom: after the conquest the Incas carried Chimú metalworkers to Cusco to make gold and silver ornaments for their temples and palaces, and sent others to the region of Lake Titicaca. Many archaeologists believe that Chimor also gave the Incas a model for some of their own political and economic arrangements, and the Chimú practice of split inheritance has been compared with the Inca custom of preserving the palaces and estates of dead rulers. Because Chimor inherited much from the Moche and the Sicán, it carried north-coast traditions of irrigation, monumental adobe building and metalworking into the Inca and colonial periods. Chan Chan, damaged by looting, rain and modern building, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986 and placed at the same time on the List of World Heritage in Danger.

Wari’s economy rested on highland farming. Its settlers spread terraced and irrigated fields through the valleys they occupied: in the Carhuarazo valley, Katharina Schreiber found that Wari rule brought new terraces and a shift from tubers alone to tubers and maize. Llamas and alpacas supplied wool, meat and transport, and feasting deposits suggest that camelids were also prized as a form of wealth. Maize beer, or chicha, and a spicy beer brewed from the berries of the molle tree were central to political life. On Cerro Baúl in the Moquegua valley, archaeologists led by Patrick Ryan Williams found a brewery with more than twenty vats, where Wari lords probably hosted feasts that bound local leaders to the state. Craft production reached a high standard. Workshops at Conchopata fired large polychrome vessels in kilns, and weavers made tapestry tunics with cotton warps and dyed camelid-fibre wefts, some woven at more than 100 threads to the inch, whose standardised, deliberately compressed designs probably came from state-sponsored workshops. Metalworkers used silver, copper, gold and arsenical bronze. Society was strongly ranked: large elite compounds and richly furnished tombs contrast with simple burials, and the mausoleum at El Castillo de Huarmey shows that noblewomen could command great wealth.
Its tapestry tunics, pottery and Staff God imagery travelled widely, and feasts with maize and molle beer helped bind local leaders to the state.

The Purépecha Empire, called the Tarascan state by the Spaniards, grew up around Lake Pátzcuaro in the volcanic highlands of Michoacán, in western Mexico. Its early history is known chiefly from the Relación de Michoacán, compiled around 1539–1541, probably by the Franciscan friar Jerónimo de Alcalá, for Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza from the testimony of Purépecha nobles and priests. In this account a lineage called the uacúsecha, ‘eagles’, of Chichimec origin, entered the region near Zacapu and moved to the shores of the lake, where they contended with the other lords of the basin. In the fourteenth century their leader Tariácuri, lord of Pátzcuaro, brought the lake communities under his control through war and alliance. He divided his realm among three heirs, his son Hiquíngare at Pátzcuaro and his nephews Hiripan at Ihuatzio and Tangáxoan at Tzintzuntzan, who carried the conquests beyond the basin. Archaeology broadly agrees with this outline: the state took shape in the Pátzcuaro basin in the fourteenth century, when the population of the basin was growing rapidly, and its rulers fostered a new state religion and ideology to support their authority. By the middle of the fifteenth century power was concentrated at Tzintzuntzan, which remained the capital until the Spanish conquest.

The Republic of Colombia was created by the constitution of 1886, which replaced the Liberal federation of the United States of Colombia set up by the Rionegro constitution of 1863. Under that charter nine sovereign states held most power, and quarrels between them, the Radical Liberals and the Catholic Church produced repeated civil wars. Rafael Núñez of Cartagena, a Liberal who was president in 1880–1882 and again from 1884, promoted a programme he called the Regeneration, aimed at order, central authority and reconciliation with the Church, and drew closer to the Conservatives. When the Radicals rose against him in 1884–1885 and were defeated, Núñez announced that the constitution of 1863 had ceased to exist. A National Council of Delegates, two from each state, drafted a new charter whose principal author was the Conservative scholar Miguel Antonio Caro; it was proclaimed in August 1886. The states became departments under governors appointed by the president, the presidential term was extended from two to six years, Catholicism was declared the religion of the nation, and the death penalty was restored except for political crimes. A concordat with the Holy See in 1887 returned much of the Church’s influence, including a leading role in education. Amended many times, the constitution lasted until 1991, longer than any other in Colombia’s history.

Mapungubwe set the pattern for the states that followed it on the plateau north of the Limpopo. The separation of a sacred ruler from his subjects and the use of stone walls to mark royal space reappeared at Great Zimbabwe and later at Khami and other centres of the Zimbabwe tradition. Mapungubwe also shows how early the interior of southern Africa was linked to the Indian Ocean economy, a connection that brought Indian beads and Chinese celadon to the Limpopo centuries before Europeans arrived. Recent excavations at Mapela Hill in south-western Zimbabwe, where a hilltop elite may have lived up to two centuries earlier, have reopened the question of where the first such state arose. Mapungubwe was long remembered locally as a sacred hill that should not be climbed. Around New Year 1933 a local guide led the farmer E.S.J. van Graan, his son and others up the hill, where they found gold objects, and the University of Pretoria began excavating in 1933. For decades the finds received little public attention. Since the end of apartheid Mapungubwe has become a national symbol: the Order of Mapungubwe, instituted in 2002, is South Africa’s highest honour and its badge shows the golden rhinoceros, and the Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003.

Ndongo’s most lasting mark is a name: the Portuguese called the ngola’s country Angola, and the colony founded at Luanda in 1576 grew into the modern state that kept it. The kingdom’s wars also shaped the early Atlantic world. Captives from the Portuguese campaigns against Ndongo were shipped from Luanda in large numbers, and the historian John Thornton has argued that the ‘20. and odd Negroes’ landed at Point Comfort in English Virginia in August 1619 were probably among the thousands captured in 1618–1619, taken from Luanda on a slave ship bound for Veracruz and seized at sea by English privateers. Linda Heywood and John Thornton have argued that Central Africans of this kind, many of them familiar with Christianity and Portuguese ways, formed the first generations of Africans in the English and Dutch colonies of the Americas. Njinga became one of the best-documented African rulers of her century, the subject of biographies by the Capuchin missionaries Antonio da Gaeta, published in 1669, and Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi, who knew her court. European writers of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries turned her into a figure of exotic cruelty, but in the twentieth century she became a symbol of resistance during the Angolan War of Independence. A statue of her stands in Kinaxixi Square in Luanda, and she is honoured in Angola as a national heroine.

Nri left a deeper mark on Igbo culture than its size suggests. The Ozo title system spread through northern Igboland under Nri’s ritual sponsorship and became one of the main ladders of social advancement for Igbo men, and the ichi marks of titled men, the yam rites and the rules of abomination and cleansing that Nri agents enforced became widespread. The traditions of origin of the Umueri clans centre on Nri and Aguleri, the communities descended from Eri, which many Igbo remember as an ancestral and religious centre. The Igbo-Ukwu finds, whatever their exact relation to Nri, rank among the masterpieces of early African metalwork. Cast in bronze by the lost-wax method, they include a vessel modelled as a pot enclosed in rope on a stand, pendants in the form of human, ram and elephant heads, and objects encrusted with insects, beads and fine relief, and one pendant head bears facial lines resembling ichi marks. They show that a society in the forest zone of West Africa produced sophisticated metalwork centuries before European contact, in a tradition distinct from the later ones of Ife and Benin. Nri is remembered today as a cradle of Igbo civilisation, and its history was reconstructed in detail by Onwuejeogwu in An Igbo Civilization: Nri Kingdom and Hegemony (1981).

Military power rested on the princes and chiefs, who owed the mwami contingents of fighting men in time of war; commoners could be called up, and warriors fought on foot with spears, bows and shields. These forces carried the expansion of the early nineteenth century, when Ntare IV Rugamba annexed southern Bugesera and lands to the east and south and fought Rwanda on the northern frontier. After his death they were turned inward, as Mwezi IV Gisabo (r. c. 1850–1908), who came to the throne as a boy, fought his elder brothers and the Batare princes, descendants of Ntare who held much of the east and south. Against outsiders the kingdom proved formidable. In the mid-1880s Mwezi’s warriors defeated an attempt by Rumaliza, the Swahili-Arab trader of Ujiji, to push into Burundi. After Germany set up a military post at Usumbura on the lake shore in 1896, Mwezi refused to submit for seven years. The decisive campaign came in 1903, when Captain Robert von Beringe marched against him with askari and machine guns, supported by his rivals Kilima and Maconco. Defeated in battle, Mwezi submitted in the Treaty of Kiganda.

Like Rwanda, Burundi is one of the few African countries whose borders largely follow those of a precolonial kingdom, and nearly all Burundians, Hutu, Tutsi and Twa alike, speak one language, Kirundi. The kingdom also showed unusual staying power. It kept the slave-trading networks of the nineteenth century at bay, resisted German conquest for years and, unlike the monarchy of neighbouring Rwanda, which was swept away in 1959–1961, survived colonial rule to bring the country to independence. Prince Louis Rwagasore, eldest son of Mwambutsa IV, who led the nationalist party UPRONA to victory in 1961, is honoured as the hero of independence, and the anniversary of his death, 13 October, is a public holiday. The royal culture outlived the throne. The drums of the court sanctuaries, played by drummers descended from the families who guarded them, became Burundi’s best-known art; Burundian drummers toured abroad from the 1960s, and in 2014 UNESCO inscribed the ritual dance of the royal drum on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The colonial period left a heavier legacy: European writers read the kingdom through racial theories that cast the Tutsi as foreign conquerors, an interpretation historians now reject, and colonial administration hardened social categories that had once been more fluid.

The Etruscans of central Italy built rich, independent city-states from about 900 BCE, traded with Greeks and Carthaginians, and created a distinctive art of painted tombs, bronzes and terracottas. They left a deep mark on early Rome, which conquered their cities in the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE and absorbed their people, while their religion and arts influenced Roman civilisation for centuries.

The Maya shared in Mesoamerican religion, the tradition of gods of rain, maize and the sun, of sacred calendars and of offerings of blood that bound together the peoples of the region, but they gave it their own forms. Among their gods were Itzamna, an aged creator associated with the sky and with writing; Chaac, the god of rain and lightning; K’awiil, a god of lightning and abundance whose image kings held as a sceptre; the young maize god, whose death and rebirth mirrored the farming year; the sun god, K’inich Ajaw; and the lords of Xibalba, the underworld. The world was imagined in layers, with a great tree at its centre and a colour and gods for each of its four directions.

Kings stood at the centre of religious life. They let their own blood as offerings, danced in the guise of gods, called up the spirits of ancestors and marked the endings of periods of time, above all the twenty-year k’atun, with ceremonies and new monuments. Dead kings were buried within temples raised over their tombs, like that of K’inich Janaab Pakal at Palenque, and honoured as ancestors. Caves, as entrances to the underworld, and cenotes, as sources of water and rain, were sacred: the Sacred Cenote at Chichén Itzá received offerings of jade, gold, copal incense and human lives. The ballgame, played in courts at the heart of the cities, echoed the struggles of the myths, and captives were sacrificed on great occasions.

Much of this is known from the Maya themselves: inscriptions that name the gods and describe royal rituals, scenes painted on pottery, the almanacs of the surviving books, and the Popol Vuh, written down by K’iche' nobles in the 1550s, which tells of the making of the first people from maize and of the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, who defeated the lords of Xibalba. Spanish friars such as Diego de Landa described the ceremonies of Yucatán even as they suppressed them. Much survived the conquest, and in highland Guatemala Maya day-keepers still count the 260-day calendar and hold ceremonies at mountains and caves.

The Mississippian culture, from about 800 to 1600, was the way of life of many Native American peoples of the Mississippi valley and the South-East: maize farmers ruled by hereditary chiefs from towns of earthen platform mounds, Cahokia the greatest. Its art and ceremonies left a lasting mark, and its peoples, broken by war, disease and slave raids after European contact, rebuilt themselves as the nations of the South-East.

The terracottas are the culture’s great achievement. They range from small figures to heads and bodies close to life size, and they show men and women standing or seated and, much more rarely, animals. They were made of coarse-grained clay, built up by hand in coils around a hollow interior, coated with a slip and burnished, and fired at low temperatures in open fires fed with grass, twigs and leaves. Their style is distinctive and remarkably consistent. The heads are large in proportion to the bodies; the eyes, usually triangular or semicircular beneath arching brows, have pierced pupils, and nostrils, ears and mouths are often pierced as well. Hairstyles are modelled in great detail, with buns, crests and plaits, and many figures wear necklaces, bracelets and anklets of beads. Their combination of strict stylisation with lifelike detail has made them widely admired, and they are counted among the masterpieces of early African art.

Making such large hollow figures without cracking them in the firing demanded great skill, and the number of fragments points to a long tradition of practised makers, though how and where they worked is not known. The Nok people also made everyday pottery, whose changing shapes and decoration over some fifteen centuries are the basis of the modern chronology, and they used grinding stones and wore beads of stone. No writing is known from the culture.

The Nok people were also among the early ironworkers of West Africa. At Taruga, a trial excavation of eight days in January 1961 uncovered the bases and walls of smelting furnaces still in place, with slag, fragments of tuyères, the clay pipes that carried air into a furnace, and objects of wrought iron; radiocarbon dates from the site point to about the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE. More recent work suggests that iron smelting began in the Nok region during the Middle Nok phase, perhaps between about 750 and 550 BCE, though the dating of early African iron is much debated. Grinding stones and other stone tools remained in use alongside the new metal.

Under the Abbasid caliphs and then the Samanids, who ruled from Samarkand and later Bukhara between about 819 and 999, Sogdiana became one of the heartlands of the Islamic world, and the Samanid court at Bukhara was a cradle of New Persian literature. The Sogdians converted to Islam, and in the towns their language gave way to Persian, which survives there as Tajik, and later in many places to Turkic. Sogdian religious texts were still copied at Turfan and Dunhuang in the 9th and 10th centuries, and around 1000 the scholar al-Biruni, from neighbouring Khwarazm, recorded the Sogdian calendar and festivals; by the 11th century the Sogdians had merged into the Persian- and Turkic-speaking peoples of Central Asia. One Sogdian dialect survives: Yaghnobi, thought to descend from the speech of the principality of Ushrusana, is still spoken by the Yaghnobis of Tajikistan.

The Sogdians’ most lasting legacy was their alphabet. In the 8th century the Uyghurs adopted it, and from the Old Uyghur script came the traditional Mongolian script and, under Nurhaci, the Manchu script. An alphabet of the Persian chancery, carried across Asia by Sogdian merchants, is thus still written in Inner Mongolia today.

Modern knowledge of the Sogdians was rebuilt almost entirely in the 20th century: from the Ancient Letters and the religious texts of Turfan and Dunhuang, from the Mount Mugh archive, from the Soviet excavations at Panjikent and the discovery of the Afrasiab paintings in 1965, and from the tombs of Sogdian families excavated in northern China, above all those found at Xi’an and Taiyuan since 1999. Historians such as Étienne de la Vaissière have reconstructed their network of merchant colonies, and the Sogdians, once seen as obscure go-betweens, are now recognised as the leading traders of the Silk Road between the 4th and 8th centuries and as a civilisation in their own right, whose painting, music and religious life left their mark from Persia to China.

Viking-Age society was built on the farm. Most Scandinavians were free farmers who raised cattle, sheep, pigs, barley and oats, fished, hunted and made iron from bog ore, living in long houses where people and animals often shared one roof. Above them stood chieftains, jarls and kings, whose power rested on land, gifts and loyal warriors; below them were thralls, slaves, many of them captives taken in raids. Free men settled disputes and made decisions at assemblies called things. In Iceland, which had no king, the Althing met each summer at Þingvellir from about 930, with a law-speaker who recited the law.

Women ran the household and its stores, and keys are common in their graves; later law codes and sagas show women owning property and seeking divorce. Some were buried with great honour, like the two women laid in the Oseberg ship in 834. A warrior’s grave at Birka in Sweden, long assumed to be a man’s, was shown by DNA in 2017 to be a woman’s, though what this means is debated. Children worked on the farm from an early age, and fostering children in other households bound families together.

Trade grew alongside raiding. Market towns, Ribe, Hedeby at the base of Jutland, Birka on Lake Mälaren and Kaupang in Norway, drew craftsmen who made combs, beads, jewellery and weapons, and merchants who dealt in furs, walrus ivory, amber, slaves and silver. Silver was weighed rather than counted: coins, ingots and jewellery were cut into pieces and nicked to test their purity, and hoards of this hack-silver, rich in Islamic dirhams, have been found across Scandinavia, above all on the island of Gotland. Kings learned to profit from trade and to protect it, as the Danish king Godfred did when he strengthened the Danevirke, the earthwork across the base of Jutland, around 808.

Viking art is an art of ornament, above all of animals: gripping beasts, ribbon-like serpents and stylised creatures twist across wood, metal and stone. Art historians name a sequence of styles after find-places, Oseberg, Borre, Jelling, Mammen, Ringerike and Urnes, running from about 800 into the 12th century, when the carved portal of the Urnes Stave Church in Norway shows the last of them. The Oseberg burial of 834 preserved the finest early woodwork: the ship’s spiralling prow, a carved cart, sledges and animal-head posts. Smiths made the paired oval brooches that held a woman’s dress, arm rings and the Mammen axe, inlaid with silver, and Harald Bluetooth’s runestone at Jelling bears an early image of Christ.

The ships were the age’s great technical achievement. Built of overlapping oak planks on a keel, light and flexible, with a square sail and oars, they could cross open sea, run up shallow rivers and land on beaches. The Gokstad ship of about 890 is some 23 metres long, and a replica crossed the Atlantic in 1893. The Skuldelev ships, sunk as a barrier in Roskilde Fjord in Denmark and raised between 1957 and 1962, include a warship some 30 metres long built near Dublin about 1042 and a sturdy cargo ship from western Norway. Navigators steered without a compass, by the sun and stars, coastlines, birds and whales.

The Vikings wrote in the younger futhark, a runic alphabet of sixteen letters in use from about 800, cut into wood, bone and stone. Thousands of runestones, most raised in the late 10th and 11th centuries and most of them in Sweden, commemorate the dead and the journeys on which some died, in England, in “Greece”, meaning Byzantium, or in Serkland, the Islamic lands. Poetry was the most admired art. Skalds composed praise poems for kings in intricate metres, rich in kennings, riddling poetic names for things; this verse, the mythological and heroic poems of the Edda and the prose sagas of kings and of Icelandic families were written down in Iceland between the 12th and 14th centuries.

Albert Luthuli (c. 1898–1967), a Zulu chief deposed by the government for his politics, led the ANC from 1952 and received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1960. Nelson Mandela (1918–2013), a lawyer who opened a practice with Oliver Tambo in Johannesburg in 1952, was “volunteer-in-chief” of the Defiance Campaign and the first commander of Umkhonto we Sizwe, and in twenty-seven years in prison, eighteen of them on Robben Island, he became the world’s best-known political prisoner. Walter Sisulu, the ANC’s secretary-general and Mandela’s mentor, was imprisoned with him; Oliver Tambo (1917–1993) left the country in 1960 and led the ANC in exile for three decades. Robert Sobukwe (1924–1978), the PAC’s leader, was held on Robben Island for six years under a law passed to keep him there, then confined to Kimberley until his death. Steve Biko (1946–1977), a medical student, founded the South African Students’ Organisation in 1968 and gave Black Consciousness its voice.

Women were at the heart of the struggle. Lilian Ngoyi and Helen Joseph led the Women’s March of 1956, Albertina Sisulu became one of the presidents of the UDF, and Winnie Madikizela-Mandela, banished to a small town in the Free State from 1977 to 1985, kept her husband’s name before the world, though the Truth and Reconciliation Commission later held her politically and morally accountable for crimes committed by her bodyguards, the Mandela United Football Club. The churches gave the movement shelter and a voice: Desmond Tutu, general secretary of the South African Council of Churches and from 1986 Archbishop of Cape Town, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984, and the Afrikaner minister Beyers Naudé left the ministry of his church to found the Christian Institute in 1963. White opponents of apartheid included the communist lawyer Bram Fischer, who defended Mandela at Rivonia and died a prisoner, the writer Ruth First, killed by a parcel bomb sent by the security police to Maputo in 1982, and Helen Suzman, for thirteen years the only member of her party in parliament.

Abroad, the Anglican priest Trevor Huddleston, who had worked in Sophiatown until 1956, became president of the British Anti-Apartheid Movement, and Julius Nyerere of Tanzania and Kenneth Kaunda of Zambia gave the exiled movements bases. Yet the movement’s strength lay with millions of ordinary people: the women who resisted the passes, the workers who built trade unions, the students of 1976, the township youth of the 1980s, and the prisoners, exiles and their families, who paid for resistance with their liberty and often their lives.

The labour movement, born with industry in Britain around 1800, organised wage-earners in trade unions, cooperatives and parties to win better pay, shorter hours, security and political rights. Persecuted at first, it spread across the world, won the eight-hour day, social insurance and a place in government, and left a lasting mark on law, politics and everyday working life.

The Romantics changed the arts for good. They made lyric poetry the voice of personal experience, developed the historical novel and the tale of terror and the fantastic, raised landscape painting to the first rank and made new forms central to music: the art song, the short piano piece, the programme symphony and later the symphonic poem. Their love of the past fostered new branches of scholarship. The Grimms studied the history of the German language as well as its tales, scholars across Europe collected ballads and edited medieval epics, and historians such as Jules Michelet wrote vivid narrative histories of their nations. Architects revived the Gothic: work on Cologne Cathedral, left unfinished since the late Middle Ages, resumed in 1842 and was completed in 1880, and after the fire of 1834 the Palace of Westminster was rebuilt in Gothic style by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin.

Romanticism also helped to make nations. European sympathy for the Greeks, roused by Byron and the philhellenes, helped bring the intervention of Britain, France and Russia that led to the Battle of Navarino in 1827 and to Greek independence. Under the partitions, Polish poets and musicians kept alive a national culture without a state, and Giuseppe Mazzini, who founded Young Italy in 1831, preached the brotherhood of free nations. Finns, Czechs, Hungarians and others turned their languages into vehicles of literature and national pride.

Its weaknesses showed too. The cult of genius could excuse self-absorption, and the love of the national past could turn into hostility towards neighbours and minorities. The revolutions of 1848–1849 failed almost everywhere: Petőfi fell in battle in July 1849 and many Romantic exiles never went home. By the 1850s Realism in painting and the novel, represented by Gustave Courbet and later Gustave Flaubert, and confidence in positive science had displaced Romantic idealism. In music the Romantic style lived on through Richard Wagner, Johannes Brahms and Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky to the end of the century.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton, the movement’s leading thinker in America, drafted the Declaration of Sentiments and began, with Anthony and Matilda Joslyn Gage, the History of Woman Suffrage, which Ida Husted Harper completed in six volumes in 1922; her Woman’s Bible (1895–1898), a critique of the scriptures’ teaching on women, was formally disowned by the national association in 1896. Susan B. Anthony, a veteran of the temperance and anti-slavery campaigns, organised and lectured for half a century; arrested for voting in the presidential election of 1872, she was fined $100 at her trial in 1873 and refused to pay. Lucy Stone kept her own name after marriage and founded the Woman’s Journal in 1870. Sojourner Truth, who had freed herself from slavery, spoke at a women’s rights convention in Akron, Ohio, in 1851; the famous version of her speech, with its refrain “Ain’t I a woman?”, was published by Frances Dana Gage only in 1863 and differs from reports made at the time.

African American women built their own organisations, from the National Association of Colored Women, founded in 1896 with Mary Church Terrell as its president, to the Alpha Suffrage Club that the journalist Ida B. Wells founded in Chicago in 1913. The last generation in the United States was led by Carrie Chapman Catt, a formidable organiser who headed both the national association and the International Woman Suffrage Alliance, and Alice Paul, who had been imprisoned and force-fed with the British suffragettes and brought their tactics home.

In Britain, Lydia Becker of Manchester led the early societies and Millicent Garrett Fawcett the non-militant National Union from 1897 to 1919. Emmeline Pankhurst and her daughters Christabel, the chief strategist of the Women’s Social and Political Union, and Sylvia, who broke away to organise working women in the East End of London, led the militants; Annie Kenney, a former cotton-mill worker, was among their best-known speakers. In New Zealand Kate Sheppard wrote pamphlets and organised the petitions of 1891–1893. Elsewhere the leaders included Vida Goldstein in Australia, Aletta Jacobs in the Netherlands, Bertha Lutz in Brazil, Huda Sha’arawi in Egypt and Ichikawa Fusae in Japan. Most of the work, however, was done by people whose names are seldom remembered: women who carried petitions from door to door, sold newspapers on street corners, chalked pavements and marched, many of them textile workers in the north of England, and men such as Frederick Douglass who stood with them.

At the heart of bhakti was the conviction that God, whether Vishnu in one of his forms, above all Krishna and Rama, or Shiva, could be known and loved as a person, and that such love, freely given and answered by divine grace, led to liberation more surely than sacrifice, learning or austerity. The devotee might approach God as a servant approaches a master, a child its parent, a friend a friend or a lover the beloved. Many poets sang of a particular image in a particular temple: Ranganatha at Srirangam, Vithoba at Pandharpur, Jagannath at Puri. Others, the sants of northern India such as Kabir and Ravidas, worshipped God without form or attributes, nirguna, whom no image or scripture could contain, in contrast to the saguna devotion to a god with form.

The means were open to all: singing and repeating the names of God, hearing the songs of the saints, keeping company with fellow devotees, pilgrimage and service to a guru. The Bhagavata Purana, whose final form many scholars date to the 9th or early 10th century and trace to the south, carried this devotion to Krishna into Sanskrit and became its great scripture. Teachers gave the devotion a philosophy. Ramanuja, traditionally dated 1017–1137, taught at Srirangam that souls and the world are real and form the body of God, a system known as Vishishtadvaita, qualified non-dualism, which he set against the strict non-dualism of Adi Shankara. Madhvacharya taught that God and souls are for ever distinct. In the 16th century Vallabha preached a path of grace, and Chaitanya’s followers at Vrindavan, above all Rupa and Sanatana Goswami, set out a theology that analysed the emotions of love for Krishna.

The saints spoke and sang in the languages of ordinary people, and many declared that before God birth, caste, sex and learning counted for nothing. Some went further. The vachanas of Basava’s circle in Karnataka rejected caste distinctions and temple ritual, and Kabir mocked the pride of Brahmin and mullah alike. Yet most saints sought a change of heart rather than a new social order, and many of the movement’s teachers were themselves Brahmins who wrote in Sanskrit as well as in the vernaculars. How far the movement set out to challenge caste, or the authority of the Vedas and of Sanskrit, remains one of the main questions that historians debate.

Rifa’a al-Tahtawi (1801–1873), from Tahta in Upper Egypt, was the first great figure: a scholar trained at al-Azhar who learned French in Paris, translated and supervised the translation of many books, and wrote on the education of girls and boys alike. Butrus al-Bustani (1819–1883), born to a Maronite family in Mount Lebanon, became a Protestant and taught, translated and founded schools, journals and works of reference; his family carried on the encyclopedia after his death. Nasif al-Yaziji (1800–1871) revived the classical maqama in his Majma' al-bahrayn, and his son Ibrahim and daughter Warda were writers in their turn. Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq (c. 1805–1887), also born a Maronite in Mount Lebanon, worked in Cairo, Malta, England and France; his extraordinary book al-Saq 'ala al-saq, “Leg over Leg”, published in Paris in 1855, mixed autobiography, satire and play with words. He later became a Muslim and settled in Istanbul.

In the next generation Jamal al-Din al-Afghani (1838/9–1897), a restless teacher who lived in Cairo in the 1870s, and his disciple Muhammad Abduh (1849–1905) led the reform of Islamic thought, and Abduh’s pupil Rashid Rida (1865–1935) carried it on in al-Manar. Abd al-Rahman al-Kawakibi (1854–1902) of Aleppo wrote against tyranny. Jurji Zaydan (1861–1914), a Beiruti who settled in Cairo, edited al-Hilal and wrote popular historical novels and a history of Islamic civilisation; Ya’qub Sarruf and Faris Nimr edited al-Muqtataf, which brought modern science, Darwin’s theory among it, before Arab readers. The poets Mahmud Sami al-Barudi and Ahmad Shawqi renewed classical poetry. Women wrote and edited: the poet Aisha Taymur, the biographer Zaynab Fawwaz, the editor Hind Nawfal and, at the end of the period, Malak Hifni Nasif.

Behind them stood a wider public of teachers, printers, booksellers, subscribers and readers, members of learned and literary societies, and the pupils of the new schools. It remained a minority: most people in Egypt and Syria could not read, and the Nahda was at first the work of an urban elite, many of them Christians from Lebanon and Syria with access to mission schools and to foreign languages.

The classical case for aristocracy rested on the idea that government is a skill and a moral calling that few possess. Plato argued that just as not everyone can navigate a ship or practise medicine, so only those trained to know the good should rule, and both he and Aristotle held that true rule by the best surpassed rule by the many. Aristotle valued the leisure, education and experience that let a few citizens devote themselves to public life. Polybius set out to explain how Rome had come to rule almost the whole known world in under fifty-three years, and he placed his account of its constitution after his narrative of the Battle of Cannae in 216 BCE, crediting the balance of Senate, consuls and people with Rome’s recovery from that disaster.

Later defenders stressed the nobility’s role as a check on power. Montesquieu, in The Spirit of the Laws (1748), saw the nobility as the most natural of the “intermediate powers” that kept a monarchy from becoming a despotism, summing up its place in the maxim “no monarch, no nobility; no nobility, no monarch”. Edmund Burke defended a “natural aristocracy” of men raised to public responsibility, and property handed down within families, as sources of continuity and prudence against revolutionary experiment. Alexis de Tocqueville argued in Democracy in America that aristocratic bodies had protected liberty against the central power, and that democracies needed voluntary associations to take their place. Even Thomas Jefferson agreed, in a letter to John Adams in 1813, that there was a “natural aristocracy” among men, grounded in “virtue and talents”, although he wanted it chosen by election rather than by birth.

Defenders also pointed to results. Venice’s patricians governed a stable republic for five centuries after closing their ruling council, serving the state in short and often poorly paid offices. The peers and gentry who governed Britain in the 18th and 19th centuries presided over constitutional stability, commercial and imperial expansion and the first industrial revolution, while the gentry ran county government without pay as justices of the peace. Families rooted in their estates, their defenders argued, took a longer view than politicians who depended on the next election.

Political thinkers have long tied self-government to small size. Aristotle defined the citizen as one who shares in judging and ruling, and held that a city must be small enough for its citizens to know one another’s characters if they are to choose officials and judge disputes well. Montesquieu argued in The Spirit of the Laws (1748) that it is natural for a republic to have only a small territory, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who signed himself a citizen of Geneva, held in The Social Contract (1762) that a people could make its own laws only in a state small enough for it to assemble. Classical Athens, where thousands of citizens attended the assembly and served on the council and in the courts, was their great example.

City-states have also been credited with remarkable economic and cultural creativity. Northern Italy became the most urban and commercial region of medieval Europe, and the chronicler Giovanni Villani reckoned that some 8,000 to 10,000 Florentine children were learning to read around 1338. Leonardo Fibonacci’s Liber Abaci (1202) taught merchants Hindu-Arabic arithmetic, Italian merchants developed double-entry bookkeeping, set out in print by Luca Pacioli in 1494, and Florentine humanists such as Leonardo Bruni praised their republic’s liberty as the source of its greatness, an outlook the historian Hans Baron called civic humanism. Athens and Florence, both city-states, gave Europe much of what it later counted as its classical inheritance.

Defenders also point to the stability and cooperation some city-states achieved. Aristotle praised the constitution of Carthage, noting that it had suffered no rebellion worth mentioning and no tyrant. The Republic of Venice kept its institutions, from the elected doge to the Great Council, for five centuries after 1297, and writers such as Gasparo Contarini held it up as a model of balanced mixed government. The Hanseatic towns, with no common government, settled their affairs by consensus at their diets, spread a common town law from Lübeck and for three centuries kept the trade of the Baltic and the North Sea largely in their hands.

The city-state, a city that governs itself and its countryside, was among the earliest forms of state and one of the most inventive. From Uruk and Athens to Kilwa, Venice and Lübeck it fostered citizenship, commerce and republican thought, though its small size left it prone to faction and conquest; Singapore, Monaco and Vatican City carry it on today.
Small size fostered participation, trade and invention but left city-states open to faction and conquest; Singapore, Monaco and Vatican City are their sovereign heirs today.

Defenders of constitutional monarchy have argued above all that it separates the dignity of the state from the business of government. Walter Bagehot divided the English constitution into “dignified” parts, which win the loyalty and reverence of the people, and “efficient” parts, which govern: the monarchy supplied the first so that the cabinet could do the second, and attachment to a family on the throne lent stability to ministries that changed with elections. Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, in his Elements of the Philosophy of Right (1820), argued that a hereditary monarch with limited powers best embodied the unity of the state and gave it continuity in emergencies, because a crown that passed by birth was no prize for factions. Edmund Burke, in his Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790), defended the Revolution of 1688 as “made to preserve our ancient indisputable laws and liberties”, a model of change that kept inherited institutions.

Supporters also point to the form’s record. Britain moved from royal government to parliamentary democracy without revolution after 1688, and the Scandinavian kingdoms, the Netherlands and Belgium extended the vote and built welfare states under the crown. The sociologist Seymour Martin Lipset observed in Political Man (1960) that most of the stable democracies of Europe and the English-speaking world were monarchies, and argued that keeping the crown had helped conservative groups to accept democratic change. Monarchs have at times defended constitutional government. On 23 February 1981, when officers of the Civil Guard seized the Spanish parliament, King Juan Carlos I appeared on television in uniform to order the army to uphold the constitution, and the attempted coup collapsed. Supporters of the Australian Governor-General’s dismissal of the prime minister Gough Whitlam in 1975, after the Senate had blocked the budget, saw it as proof that reserve powers could break a deadlock and check politicians who exceeded their powers.

Advocates also value a head of state who stands outside party competition. A monarch trained for the role, serving for decades and owing the office to no party can, they argue, represent the whole nation, embody continuity across changes of government and act as a neutral arbiter when no party commands a majority, as the monarchs of Belgium and Denmark do when they appoint a figure to lead negotiations for a coalition after an election.

Some early modern regimes have been called dictatorships. Oliver Cromwell’s Protectorate of 1653–1658 was described as a military dictatorship by his enemies and by some modern scholars, and Maximilien Robespierre was called a dictator while the Committee of Public Safety directed the Reign of Terror in France in 1793–1794. Dictatorship became a major form of government in the 19th century. Napoleon Bonaparte’s coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 and his nephew Napoleon III’s coup of 1851 gave Europe the models of Bonapartism and Caesarism: rule by a strong man who claimed to embody the nation and confirmed his power by plebiscite. In Latin America the wars of independence were followed by the rule of caudillos, such as José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, perpetual dictator of Paraguay from 1816, and Porfirio Díaz, who governed Mexico for most of the years from 1876 to 1911.

The 20th century was the age of dictatorship. The First World War destroyed old monarchies and left new democracies unstable. The Bolsheviks seized power in Russia in 1917 and created the Soviet Union, where Joseph Stalin had established personal and totalitarian rule by 1929; Benito Mussolini came to power in Italy in 1922 and from 1925 built the first fascist dictatorship; and Adolf Hitler, appointed chancellor in January 1933, used emergency decrees and the Enabling Act of 1933 to destroy German democracy within months. Dictators also ruled Poland after Józef Piłsudski’s coup of 1926, Portugal under António de Oliveira Salazar, Spain under Francisco Franco from 1939, much of the Balkans and the Baltic states, and Brazil under Getúlio Vargas from 1937. After Nazi Germany’s defeat in 1945 the Soviet Union imposed communist dictatorships across Central and Eastern Europe, and in 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People’s Republic of China.

During the Cold War dictatorship spread across the newly independent and developing world. Officers seized power in Egypt in 1952, Brazil in 1964, Chile in 1973, when General Augusto Pinochet overthrew the elected government of Salvador Allende, and Argentina in 1976, and repeatedly in Nigeria, Ghana and many other African states; independence leaders banned rival parties; and personal rulers such as Mobutu Sese Seko in Zaire (1965–1997) and Ferdinand Marcos in the Philippines (1965–1986) held power for decades. From the 1970s a wave of democratisation brought down the dictatorships of southern Europe, then many of those in Latin America and East Asia; in 1989 the communist regimes of Central and Eastern Europe fell, and the Soviet Union itself dissolved in 1991.

Defenders of direct democracy have argued first that it makes citizens. In Pericles’ funeral speech as Thucydides reports it, the Athenians regard a man who takes no part in public affairs not as quiet but as useless, and hold that discussion is no obstacle to action but the best preparation for it. Herodotus believed that freedom had made the Athenians formidable: under the tyrants they had fought no better than their neighbours, but once free and equal in speech they became the foremost fighters in Greece. Admirers point to Athens’s record. In the century after Cleisthenes its citizens beat the Persians at the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE, helped to defeat them at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BCE, built the Parthenon and staged the dramas of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides. The political scientist Josiah Ober has argued that institutions such as the Council, which every year drew 500 citizens into government, let Athens gather knowledge spread among its people and outperform rival cities.

A second argument concerns judgement. Aristotle, no friend of radical democracy, granted that the many, though individually ordinary, may judge better together than a few experts, as a feast to which many contribute is better than one provided by a single host. The Assembly could also correct itself: in 427 BCE it voted to kill all the men of rebellious Mytilene, then reversed the decision the next day, and a second ship arrived in time to stop the massacre, although about a thousand men held responsible were still executed.

Modern advocates make the case for referendums and initiatives on similar grounds. Rousseau held that only laws a people has ratified in person are truly laws. Theodore Roosevelt and the American Progressives saw the initiative as a check on legislatures dominated by railways and other corporations. Students of Swiss politics argue that the referendum turned Switzerland into a consensus democracy: after the Catholic Conservatives had repeatedly defeated federal laws by referendum, the ruling Radicals gave them a seat in the Federal Council in 1891, and from 1959 the four largest parties shared its seven seats by a fixed formula. Economists such as Lars Feld, Gebhard Kirchgässner and Bruno Frey have reported that Swiss cantons with stronger rights of popular vote tend to spend and borrow less, and that their citizens report greater satisfaction with their lives.

In the narrow sense defined by the Belgian historian François-Louis Ganshof, feudalism was a set of mutual obligations within the warrior nobility, built on three elements: the lord, the vassal and the fief. A man became a vassal through commendation: he did homage, placing his joined hands between his lord’s and declaring himself the lord’s man, and then swore fealty, an oath of fidelity, often on relics. The lord owed protection and maintenance, usually through a fief, most often land with the peasants who worked it but sometimes an office, a toll or a money rent. The vassal owed aid and counsel: military service, limited in 12th-century northern France to forty days a year on offensive campaigns, guard duty in the lord’s castle, attendance at his court to advise him and help judge disputes, and payments on set occasions.

By the middle of the 10th century fiefs had generally become hereditary, but an heir had to do homage afresh and pay a relief, and the lord kept rights that recalled his ultimate ownership: wardship of under-age heirs, the marriage of heiresses, aids to ransom him, knight his eldest son or marry his eldest daughter, and escheat, the return of the fief when a line died out. Vassals granted parts of their fiefs to vassals of their own, and many held land from several lords, which led in the 12th century to liege homage, a bond owed above all others. Beneath this structure lay the manor. In Marc Bloch’s broader picture of feudal society, peasants, many of them serfs bound to the soil, worked the lord’s demesne, paid dues in kind or money, ground their grain at his mill and answered to his court.

Feudal government divided public power among private persons. Rights of justice, taxation and command that had belonged to kings passed to counts, castellans, bishops and abbots, so that a king governed directly only his own domain and dealt with the rest of his kingdom through his great vassals. The limits on rulers were those of contract and custom: a lord who broke faith could be defied, and vassals expected to be consulted on war, law and extraordinary taxation. This distinguishes feudal monarchy from the absolute monarchies that later replaced it, which governed through salaried officials, standing armies and regular taxes, and feudalism itself from manorialism, the economic order of estates worked by dependent peasants, which was older than feudal bonds and outlasted them.

The abolition of 1789 was followed across Europe. French armies and their allies carried it into Italy, where Joseph Bonaparte abolished feudalism in the Kingdom of Naples in 1806 and the Sicilian parliament followed in 1812; Prussia began freeing its serfs in 1807, Austria abolished peasants’ labour dues in 1848 and Russia emancipated its serfs in 1861. Remnants lasted far longer: the last seigneurial rents in Quebec were paid in 1970, Scotland ended feudal land tenure only in 2004, and Sark replaced the tenants’ seats in its parliament, the Chief Pleas, with elected members in 2008. Guernsey still has fiefs whose seigneurs attend its Court of Chief Pleas, and English land law still speaks of estates held in fee simple, a descendant of the fief.

The feudal past left a double mark on European political thought. Ideas of contract, counsel and consent fed the parliaments of the later Middle Ages and the arguments of opponents of absolute monarchy, while from the Enlightenment on “feudal” became a byword for privilege and backwardness. Comparative historians have applied the term to many societies: to Japan from the Kamakura to the Tokugawa shogunates; to Zhou China, whose system of enfeoffment, fengjian, gave modern Chinese its word for feudal; to medieval Ethiopia; and to grants of revenue in return for service such as the Byzantine pronoia, the iqta of the Islamic world and the Mughal jagir. Rushton Coulborn’s Feudalism in History (1956) set such cases side by side.

Historians now argue over the word itself. In The Tyranny of a Construct (1974) Elizabeth A. R. Brown argued that feudalism was a construct of later scholars that imposed a false uniformity on the varied ties between medieval lords and their dependants, and in Fiefs and Vassals (1994) Susan Reynolds showed that the classic model of fiefs and vassalage owed much to the academic lawyers of the 12th century and after, and that earlier documents do not bear it out. Others reply that the word remains useful shorthand if carefully defined, in Ganshof’s narrow legal sense or Bloch’s broad social one, and economic historians keep it for the relation between lords and dependent peasants. Specialists on Japan such as Karl Friday now stress differences from Europe rather than similarities, and many textbooks avoid the term altogether.

Lenin and his successors argued that the working class needed a single, disciplined vanguard to take power and then to defend it: “the proletariat needs the Party first of all as its General Staff”, Joseph Stalin wrote in The Foundations of Leninism (1924). Leaders of new nations made a different case. Julius Nyerere argued in the early 1960s that rival parties suited societies divided by class, whereas in a newly independent country without such divisions they would only foster faction and tribalism, and that a single national party could still be democratic if voters chose among its candidates. In Tanzania’s election of 1965 voters in most constituencies had a choice of two candidates of the ruling party, and several ministers lost their seats.

Political scientists have found that single-party regimes are the most durable kind of dictatorship. Samuel P. Huntington argued in Political Order in Changing Societies (1968) that what modernising countries most lacked was strong institutions, and that a strong party, even a single one, could supply the order that coups and personal rulers could not. Barbara Geddes found that single-party regimes last longer than military or personal dictatorships, and Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way have argued that where a revolutionary party built the army, as in China, the armed forces have not attempted coups even after disasters such as the Great Leap Forward. Beatriz Magaloni showed how Mexico’s ruling party kept power for seven decades through elections, patronage and the co-optation of rivals rather than open terror.

Defenders also point to economic and social results. The Soviet Union industrialised rapidly and achieved near-universal literacy, and the economist Michael Ellman notes that communist states compared well with Western states on some health indicators, such as infant mortality and life expectancy; Amartya Sen observed that several made large gains in life expectancy. Since its reforms began in 1978 China has achieved rapid growth that has lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty while keeping single-party rule, and Vietnam has followed a similar path since 1986. Supporters argue that freedom from electoral cycles lets such governments plan for decades.

The collapse of 1989–1991 left both memorials and debate. Monuments to the victims of communist regimes stand in most Eastern European capitals, and museums such as the House of Terror in Budapest document both Nazi and communist rule, while scholars such as Kristen Ghodsee have recorded nostalgia for the security and welfare of the old regimes among those who lost most in the transition. Historians long debated whether the totalitarian model described the Soviet Union adequately: from the 1970s social historians stressed how much the party’s control depended on bargaining and improvisation, while the opening of the archives after 1991 confirmed the scale of its repression.

Former ruling parties often survived the change. Reformed communist parties won free elections in Lithuania in 1992, Poland in 1993 and Hungary in 1994, and several former single parties remain in power under multi-party constitutions, among them Tanzania’s Chama Cha Mapinduzi, Mozambique’s FRELIMO and Angola’s MPLA; scholars now study dominant-party and “electoral authoritarian” regimes alongside one-party states. Communist parties still rule China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea, and their constitutions give the party the leading role: Vietnam’s names the Communist Party “the leading force of the state and society”, and in 2018 China added to the first article of its constitution that the leadership of the Communist Party is the defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics. In Eritrea the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice is the only legal party.

The one-party state remains a central case for political science. Its survival in China, through rapid economic change and the protests of 1989, led the political scientist Andrew Nathan to speak of “authoritarian resilience”, while its collapse in Europe is often cited as evidence that such systems adapt poorly. The contrast between single-party rule and multi-party democracy, between unity under one organisation and competition among several, remains one of the main dividing lines in the comparison of modern governments.

A tyrant, in the Greek sense, was a man who made himself sole ruler of a city-state by means outside its customary order. The word described how power had been won, not how it was used: the Greeks called both usurpers and the sons who inherited their rule tyrants, and in the Archaic period the title carried little of its later reproach. Most tyrants came from the aristocracy. They rose by exploiting feuds among the leading families and the grievances of poorer citizens, small farmers and the newly prosperous, and many had military reputations: Peisistratus had captured the Megarian port of Nisaea before he made his bid for power in Athens.

Once in power a tyrant ruled through force, patronage and continuity. He kept a bodyguard, often of foreign mercenaries; Peisistratus began with a guard of club-bearers voted him by the Athenian assembly and later relied on hired troops paid from the gold and silver of the Mount Pangaeus region. He sent rivals into exile, held their children as hostages, placed relatives and friends in the city’s offices and made alliances by marriage and with tyrants in other cities. Yet many tyrants left the laws and magistracies in place. According to Herodotus, Peisistratus governed without disturbing the existing offices or changing the laws, and Thucydides wrote that his family took care only that one of their own always held office. Tyrants taxed harvests, built temples, fountains and harbours, founded festivals, struck coins and invited poets to their courts.

Greek political thinkers set tyranny against kingship. A king, in their view, ruled willing subjects according to law and ancestral custom and for the common good; a tyrant ruled unwilling subjects for his own advantage and above the law. Tyranny also differed from the office of the aisymnetes, a ruler given extraordinary powers by the citizens’ own choice, such as Pittacus of Mytilene, whose office Aristotle called “an elective tyranny”. The so-called Thirty Tyrants who ruled Athens in 404–403 BCE were in fact an oligarchy, a board of thirty men given the name for their lawless violence.

Bell Beaker people travelled by sea and river. From the Tagus estuary the first moves were by sea: south into the Mediterranean, with enclaves in south-western Spain, southern France and the Po Valley, and north to Brittany, from where routes along the Loire and Seine brought maritime beakers to the Lower Rhine about 2600 BCE. The spread along these long-used sea routes seems to have been linked directly to the search for copper and other rare raw materials. On the Rhine Beaker groups met the Corded Ware culture, and from there they spread east as far as the Vistula in Poland; another expansion reached Csepel Island in Hungary by about 2500 BCE.

How the culture spread is its central question. Gordon Childe pictured “missionaries” spreading copper working from Iberia, Stephen Shennan a mobile elite imposing itself, and in the mid-1970s Colin Burgess and Shennan proposed a “pots, not people” model in which local peoples adopted a package of knowledge and objects. Ancient DNA has partly resolved the debate. Olalde and colleagues (2018) found only limited genetic affinity between early Beaker people in Iberia and in central Europe, suggesting that migration played a limited role at first, but the later spread was strongly linked to migration. In Britain it brought high levels of steppe-related ancestry and replaced about 90% of the gene pool within a few centuries, and in Iberia between about 2500 and 2000 BCE about 40% of the ancestry and nearly all the male lineages were replaced by people with steppe ancestry.

Contacts reached far. Strontium analysis in Bavaria found that 18–25% of the people in Beaker graves came from well outside the area. Irish copper reached the Netherlands and Brittany, Cornish gold went to Ireland and the continent, and a glass bead from Mesopotamia was found in the Tiel enclosure. Bell Beaker artefacts appear in mainland Greece and the Aegean from about 2200–2000 BCE, and European Bronze Age ancestry, including ancestry linked to Beaker groups, has been found among the Guanches of the Canary Islands.

Exchange between coast and valleys lay at the heart of Caral–Supe. Jonathan Haas sums up the bond: the people of the valleys needed fish for protein, and the fishers needed cotton to make their nets. Which came first is long debated. In 1973 Michael E. Moseley argued that a sea-based economy laid the foundation of Andean civilisation, and that coastal Aspero was the oldest site; Haas and Shady hold that the larger inland centres developed at the same time or led. Scholars now agree that the inland sites held far more people. In 2018 David G. Beresford-Jones and colleagues defended a revised form of Moseley’s idea, in which growing cotton for nets set off the change, while the 2022 bone study found that plants, not fish, fed most people.

Caral–Supe may have stood at the centre of a wider network. Cotton fishing nets and domesticated plants have been found up and down the Peruvian coast, and reports of Shady’s work say that Caral sent its goods and those of Aspero to distant communities for Spondylus shells from Ecuador, dyes from the highlands and snuff from the Amazon, claims that should be treated with caution. Shady suggests a depiction of monkeys may point to contact with the Amazon. By around 2200 BCE its influence reached south to the Chillón valley and the site of El Paraíso and north to the Santa valley.

No sign of warfare of any kind has been found: no fortifications, weapons, burned buildings or mutilated bodies from battle, and settlements were not built for defence. In modern times Caral–Supe has itself caused conflict among archaeologists, as Shady accused Haas and Creamer of taking too much credit for her work; their institutions cleared them of plagiarism, but the Field Museum’s science council rebuked Haas for publicity that gave her too little credit.
